source: សៀវភៅស្ដីពីដំណាំដំឡូងមី (Book on Cassava), Part 2, UNDP-supported capacity-building programme for cassava, March 2015
text:
The source identifies several causes of declining cassava root quality and yield in Cambodia: continuous replanting of cassava on the same land without crop rotation or soil amendment, progressive depletion of soil nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium as the crop is repeatedly harvested without replenishment (citing Putthacharoen et al. and separately Men Sarom and colleagues, 2014, who documented yield decline in provinces such as Kampong Cham and Pailin under continuous cropping), and erosion on sloped land further reducing fertility (citing Howeler, 2012). Recommended responses include crop rotation, soil amendment with organic matter or fertilizer, and, on sloped land, erosion-control practices.

On chip processing quality: much cassava chip processing in Cambodia is done manually using basic tools rather than organized, larger-scale facilities, which the source links to inconsistent chip quality. Poor hygiene during drying and storage (dust exposure, insect and animal contact, inadequate sun-drying) is identified as a food-safety risk affecting marketability, particularly for export markets with stricter quality requirements.

The source also discusses cyanogenic glycoside (cyanide) content, which occurs naturally in cassava roots and is generally higher in bitter varieties; proper processing (peeling, soaking, adequate drying) reduces cyanide content to safe levels for both food and feed use (citing Oliveira and colleagues, 2009). Wastewater and dust from starch/chip processing facilities are noted as potential environmental and community health concerns if not properly managed, with the source noting effluent from processing sites can travel a few hundred meters and affect nearby water sources if untreated.
caveat: Several precise supporting statistics in this section (e.g., specific national wastewater-volume or dust-generation figures, and provincial yield-decline percentages) were present in the source but not transcribed here with confidence due to dense small-numeral formatting in the scanned text; only the qualitative findings and cited-study conclusions are included. A closer re-read at higher resolution would be needed to extract those exact figures reliably.
